Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 39: Process Termination — decoding results and reaping children
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. A child stops; a parent still has work to do
Problem and first experiment

SAY
When a child stops executing, the parent's lifecycle responsibility may remain. The system retains enough termination information for the parent to discover how the child ended. Collecting that information is called reaping. A terminated but unreaped child is a zombie; it is not still running its old instructions. A long-lived supervisor that ignores every completion can accumulate this bookkeeping. Start with an ownership rule: which part of the parent collects each child's status? That rule matters when multiple threads or event handlers might wait. Completion reporting should not be scattered among callers that each assume they are the only owner.

DO
Separate execution state from retained termination bookkeeping.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.012 · 39.5 Zombie processes

------------------------------------------------------------

2. A nonzero child result can be a successful test
Problem and first experiment

SAY
This actual process test launches a child that exits zero and another that exits six. Each child is waited for and decoded through the documented macros. The supervisor regards both as correct because those were the expected test outcomes, so its own exit code is zero and it prints that the checks passed. This separates the tested program's result from the test harness's result. A nonzero child status is not automatically a bug in the test; it may be exactly the failure case being verified. No raw wait-status bit layout is assumed, and only the parent produces the stable output.

DO
Predict all three lines and the parent’s own exit status.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.006 · 39.2 Exit status

------------------------------------------------------------

3. Classify status before extracting a value
Problem and first experiment

SAY
waitpid writes an encoded status containing information about the kind of event. It does not simply store the number passed to exit. First ask WIFEXITED; only then use WEXITSTATUS. If WIFSIGNALED is true, use WTERMSIG instead. Treating every raw value as an ordinary failure code hides the difference between a program reporting invalid input and being terminated by a signal. That difference matters in diagnostics and restart policy. Job-control cases add stopped and continued states when requested, so a full shell needs more categories than a minimal run-and-wait launcher. The macros preserve that contract without hand-written bit guesses.

DO
Give one normal-exit case and one signal case to classify.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.010 · 39.4 waitpid

------------------------------------------------------------

4. Observe signal termination without guessing its number
Problem and first experiment

SAY
This demonstration terminates only its own newly created child with SIGTERM. The child explicitly restores the default disposition and unblocks the signal so an inherited mask or ignored disposition does not change the intended experiment. The parent waits and requires WIFSIGNALED plus the expected signal identity. It prints category equals signal and expected-signal equals true rather than a platform-dependent numeric signal value. The fallback child exit is a failure path if signal setup fails or control unexpectedly continues. This is a bounded termination test, not a crash demonstration and not an action against another user's process.

DO
Predict the category and explain why no ordinary exit code is printed.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.020 · Worked example — Decoding success and failure

6. Where the simple approach fails
The chapter problem

SAY
Shifting raw wait-status bits without first checking the termination category can misreport a signal termination as an ordinary exit.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Always print status.value as an exit code. A signal-killed child is then reported as if it returned normally.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Classify the termination kind first, then extract the corresponding value using the platform API. Do not invent a universal bit layout.

7. Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
The chapter problem

SAY
The enum says which interpretation of value is valid. A real wait status uses OS-defined macros to discover this category; its packed integer is not directly the exit code. Separating classification from formatting makes the result clear to callers and prevents accidental bit guesses.

A plausible alternative: A process wrapper can centralize waiting and status decoding when many call sites launch children.

8. Chapter 39 — Process Termination
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Termination ends execution, but it does not erase every trace of a process immediately. The operating system retains enough information for a parent to learn how a child finished. A robust parent separates ordinary exit, signal termination, and temporary state changes rather than interpreting a raw status integer directly. [ R17 ]

10. exit
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
The C library’s exit performs normal termination processing, including registered exit handlers and standard-I/O cleanup. Returning from main has the corresponding normal-termination effect. _exit bypasses that user-space cleanup and is appropriate for many child failure paths after fork. Neither interface returns to the caller. Choose based on the process’s lifecycle, not merely on spelling. Using normal cleanup in an exec-bound child can flush copied buffers or invoke handlers intended for the original parent program.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

11. Exit status
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
An exit status communicates a small result to the parent. Conventionally zero indicates success and nonzero indicates failure, but applications define the meaning of particular nonzero values. On the POSIX wait interfaces used here, ordinary exit status is retrieved from the appropriate encoded status through macros. Do not attempt to return a large integer or arbitrary data structure through exit status. Use a pipe, file, socket, or another explicit channel for richer results. Exit status should summarize completion, not replace a data protocol.

DO

Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

12. wait
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
wait waits for an eligible child and returns its process ID together with status information. It is useful when any child’s completion can be handled next. The parent must still inspect the status classification before extracting a particular result. A parent with several children should not assume that completion order matches creation order. Scheduling and workload determine which finishes first. Waiting for one specific slow child can delay handling other already-finished children, although it remains correct when the program deliberately chooses that policy.

DO

Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

13. waitpid
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
waitpid provides more control over which child or group is considered and whether the call blocks. With WNOHANG , a return of zero means that no matching status is currently available; it is not a child’s process ID and not an error. Retry an interrupted wait when appropriate. Check WIFEXITED before using WEXITSTATUS , and check WIFSIGNALED before using WTERMSIG . Options for stopped and continued children matter for job control, which requires a broader state machine than a simple run-and-wait launcher.

14. Zombie processes
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A zombie is a terminated process whose parent has not yet collected the retained termination information. It is not executing instructions or holding its former address space as a normal live process. It does occupy bookkeeping that should eventually be released. A long-running supervisor that never reaps children can accumulate zombies. The solution is lifecycle management, not treating zombies as ordinary running tasks to be killed again. The parent must arrange to collect child status according to the applicable process and signal rules.

DO
Ask learners to identify the state, operation, and guarantee named on this page.
Use the source panel to inspect the complete original lesson and its exact wording.

content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.012, SP39.013

15. Reaping children
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Reaping collects a child’s status and releases the retained termination bookkeeping. A parent should have one clear ownership policy for child status, especially when multiple threads or signal-driven code could attempt to wait for the same child. A common event-driven pattern treats SIGCHLD as a notification to check for available statuses and then repeatedly uses nonblocking waits until none remain. Standard signals can coalesce, so one notification must not be assumed to represent exactly one child event.

16. Decode status, not bit guesses
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
This program creates one child that exits with status 23, waits for that specific child, and verifies the status using the documented macros. Companion listing: ch39/status.c The expected output is exit=23 . The parent’s own success status is zero because the child produced the expected test result. This distinction is useful in test harnesses: the tested program can intentionally return a nonzero value while the test passes by verifying that exact behavior.

17. Reaping a child
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
When a child exits, the kernel retains a small amount of termination information so its parent can collect status with wait or waitpid . Until reaped, the child is a zombie: it is no longer executing but still occupies a process-table entry. Waiting releases that retained state.

18. Decoding success and failure
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A child that executes exit(3) communicates an exit status distinct from termination by a signal. Portable parent code uses the wait-status macros rather than assuming the raw integer returned by waitpid equals the child’s exit code. The raw status encodes multiple termination cases.

22. Normal cleanup and immediate child exit are different tools
Reason about the implementation

SAY
In C++, returning from main leaves its scope and destroys its local automatic objects before normal termination completes. Calling std::exit directly performs normal termination processing such as registered handlers and standard-I/O cleanup, but it does not unwind ordinary automatic objects on the current stack. POSIX _exit bypasses that user-space cleanup, which is useful on many exec-bound child failure paths after fork. The choice therefore belongs to lifecycle design. A child should not flush copied parent buffers accidentally, while an ordinary application should not skip required cleanup merely because _exit sounds more final. Use structured scope exits for normal C++ ownership whenever the workflow permits them.

DO
Compare scope cleanup, termination handlers, and child failure cleanup separately.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.004 · 39.1 exit

------------------------------------------------------------

23. wait and waitpid encode a supervision policy
Reason about the implementation

SAY
If a parent launches a quick child and a slow child, their completion order depends on scheduling and work, not just creation order. wait can collect an eligible child whose status is available. waitpid can deliberately target one child, as our demos do to make the checked relationship exact. Waiting for a particular slow child can delay handling another that has already finished; that may be acceptable or may hurt a responsive supervisor. The interface choice should follow the application's policy. Keep a mapping from child identity to expected task so a result is associated with the right work rather than whichever status happened to arrive first.

DO
Choose a policy for a batch harness and one for a responsive task monitor.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.008 · 39.3 wait

------------------------------------------------------------

24. Nonblocking wait has three result categories
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A nonblocking wait is useful when the parent has other work. With WNOHANG, zero means no matching status is currently available; it is neither an error nor a child identifier to remove from a table. A positive return identifies the child whose status was supplied. Minus one requires checking the error, including whether an interrupted operation should be retried under the cancellation policy. A tight loop that repeatedly gets zero can waste CPU just as a busy I/O retry can. Integrate status checks with the application's event or scheduling mechanism. The state machine must preserve running children when no completion is ready yet.

DO
Ask learners to handle positive, zero, and negative returns separately.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.010 · 39.4 waitpid

------------------------------------------------------------

25. One notification can represent several completed children
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A supervisor may use SIGCHLD to learn that child state deserves attention. It must not assume one signal equals exactly one completed child. Standard signals can coalesce while several children finish. An event-driven collector commonly checks repeatedly with nonblocking waits until no matching status remains available, then returns to other work. The signal handler itself must follow signal-safety rules; notification can be separated from the later collection work. Also avoid two independent collectors racing to reap the same child. Give status ownership to one component that updates the task table and reports completion once, even when notifications are fewer than the underlying events.

DO
Imagine three children finishing while one notification is pending.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.014 · 39.6 Reaping children

29. A terminated child still needs collection
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
A terminated child still needs collection. Copy the available termination value before discarding the stored status. Dereferencing an empty optional would violate its precondition.

Model a parent observing a child’s normal exit code 7, then reaping its termination record.

Termination and collection by the parent are separate events. Real wait status must first be classified with the platform’s macros; not every termination is a normal exit. The model removes the record only after saving the result needed by the parent.

Copy the available termination value before discarding the stored status. Dereferencing an empty optional would violate its precondition.

reset destroys the stored optional value and makes the handle empty. This models collecting a terminated child’s status, not a real wait system call.

The termination value is collected before its optional storage is reset. After collection the modeled status is no longer available.

Shifting raw wait-status bits without first checking the termination category can misreport a signal termination as an ordinary exit. In the extended lab: Always print status.value as an exit code. A signal-killed child is then reported as if it returned normally.

40. Chapter summary and maintenance
Recall and transfer

SAY
The enum says which interpretation of value is valid. A real wait status uses OS-defined macros to discover this category; its packed integer is not directly the exit code. Separating classification from formatting makes the result clear to callers and prevents accidental bit guesses.

Choose a simpler approach when its narrower contract is enough. A process wrapper can centralize waiting and status decoding when many call sites launch children.

When this system changes, retain a check that exposes the known failure: Always print status.value as an exit code. A signal-killed child is then reported as if it returned normally. Classify the termination kind first, then extract the corresponding value using the platform API. Do not invent a universal bit layout.

41. Exit status is a summary, not a data transport
Recall and transfer

SAY
A child cannot return a large structure or arbitrary integer through ordinary exit status. It is a small completion summary interpreted through the wait interface. If the parent needs a list of records, a detailed error report, or a large computation result, use a pipe, file, or another explicit channel with its own framing and validation. Then define how the status relates to that payload: for example, zero may mean a complete valid report was produced. The baseline test showed that the supervisor can succeed after observing an expected nonzero child result. Document that distinction so callers do not confuse a tested outcome with a harness malfunction.

DO
Specify both a result channel and a completion code for one task.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.006 · 39.2 Exit status

------------------------------------------------------------

42. Recall stop, classify, collect, and release
Recall and transfer

SAY
A child finishing is the beginning of the parent's completion handling, not its end. The parent collects a status, classifies it with the proper macros, associates it with the task, and releases its bookkeeping exactly once. A zombie has stopped executing but awaits that collection. Normal exit and signal termination deserve distinct diagnostics. Our first demo treated a deliberate exit six as a successful test observation; the second verified termination by the intended signal without assuming its numeric value. These habits scale to supervisors that manage many children, where missed statuses and unclear ownership become persistent resource and reporting bugs.

DO
Explain both demo outcomes from the supervisor’s point of view.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch39.json → SP39.014 · 39.6 Reaping children
